description: We're making a creative game to develop space exploration for new recruits.
summary:
GTFO (Great Time For Oxygen) is a free, cozy pixel-art mission trainer by Team Araxys. Young players become an astronaut who crash-lands on a red planet beside a dead outpost, then bring it back to life. They restore life support by repairing the oxygen plant, restore power by aligning solar mirrors to the reactor, grow food and water in a nursery, and shelter from radiation. Finally they send an SOS and wait out the real light-time delay for Earth's reply.
It meets the challenge's core systems directly: life support, radiation protection, power and food, with a communication delay and trade-offs between them. Radiation alerts follow archived NASA DONKI solar-flare and particle data. If the player is outside when a storm hits, exposure builds.
It matters because children learn what staying alive off-world demands by living through the choices, not reading about them. It runs free in a browser, or on Windows and Linux.
details:
GTFO (Great Time For Oxygen) is a free pixel-art mission trainer. You are an astronaut who crash-lands on the red planet Araxys beside a dead outpost, and you use one multitool to restore it: repair the oxygen plant and reactor, mend broken windows, align solar mirrors to power the base, grow food and water in a nursery, and shelter from radiation. The final goal is to repair the comms dish and send an SOS. The reply takes real game-clock time to arrive. Oxygen, radiation, hunger and thirst are shown as five gauges, and every repair affects the others.

Players learn why life support, power, shielding, food and communication delays matter through play, not text. It runs free in a browser or as a Windows or Linux download with nothing to install, and it uses simple controls and no combat.

We want players, especially children, to feel the trade-offs of living off-world: to learn that oxygen comes first, storms mean taking cover, and Earth can't answer instantly. Radiation warnings use real archived NASA DONKI solar-flare timing.

Tools, languages and software

Godot 4.7.2 with GDScript; Python (NumPy, Pillow, SciPy) to generate all the art; FFmpeg and open-licence recordings for sound; GitHub, Vercel, and Claude Code and Codex (an AI coding assistant) for parts of the code and the website. No special hardware: ordinary laptops and desktops.

Every map, machine and sprite is generated by code, ray-marched from shape models and drawn in one shared palette. The world is pre-rendered from four sides, so the camera can turn. Nights are truly dark, with only a suit lamp to see by. The story is told through cutscenes, including Earth's delayed reply.

Factors taken into consideration:

Age-friendly design; scientific accuracy; performance on modest computers; easy access through a link; adjustable interface size and reduced-motion support; and open-licence sound with credits.
